title: Water lilies
scientificName: Nymphaea violacea, N. gigantea; also Nelumbo and Nymphoides

identification.basis: The dictionary's kababina is 'fresh water lily'. Roth (1901) recorded the Bloomfield name for the lily rhizome and the full method of baking and husking the seeds; Palmer (1883) recorded the names and uses of the blue lily on the Mitchell. The blue lily Nymphaea violacea is recorded within 30 km of Karma Waters.

summary: **[kababina](word:kababina)** is the freshwater lily, and in Roth's 1901 list of foods the lilies belong to the dry season, with honey, while 'roots and fruits' belong to the wet [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901]. The blue lily of the north, *Nymphaea*, is eaten whole: the tuber in the mud, roasted 'not unlike a potato, but yellow and dry'; the porous flower stalk, peeled and eaten raw or roasted; the flower; and the apple-sized seed pod with up to three thousand seeds, which Roth saw baked in ovens of stones or ant-bed under teatree bark, then husked by rinsing and grinding 'until such time as the water from the pasty mass is comparatively clear' [ref:palmer1883] [ref:wiki-nymphaea-gigantea] [ref:roth1901]. Roth gave the Bloomfield name of the roasted rhizome as *de-kir*, the same word used at Cooktown and Cape Bedford; Palmer, on the Mitchell, gave *Amuma* for the plant and separate names for the root, the stalk and the seed head [ref:roth1901] [ref:palmer1883]. The deep still lagoons the lilies need are where the [magpie geese](entry:waterhole), the jacana and, on the lower rivers, the crocodile also come, which is why Roth's lily-gatherers at Princess Charlotte Bay dived with a watcher on the bank [ref:wiki-nymphaea-violacea] [ref:roth1910].

infobox.label: The plant
infobox.value: Nymphaea: a tuber in the mud, round floating leaves, blue, violet or white flowers on stalks up to 50 cm above the water; the pod is drawn under water to ripen

infobox.label: Eaten
infobox.value: Tuber (roasted), flower stalk (peeled, raw or roasted), flowers, seed pod (baked), seeds (husked and ground)

infobox.label: Where
infobox.value: Permanent and semi-permanent lagoons with deep mud and at least 1.5 m of water; Nymphaea violacea recorded within 30 km of Karma Waters

infobox.label: Season
infobox.value: 'Lilies and honey in the dry season' (Roth); flowers through the year, most in the warm months

infobox.label: Watch for
infobox.value: Crocodiles in lily lagoons; a watcher on the bank when diving

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[kababina](word:kababina)** 'fresh water lily; flora and fauna belonging to the rain forest area' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[jakari](word:jakari)** 'spiderlily' is a *Crinum* of the sand and swamp edges, a different plant [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's food bulletin gives the *Nymphaea* rhizome as *de-kir* at the Bloomfield (KYE), at Cooktown and at Cape Bedford, with the seeds *nguri* at Cape Bedford and *nganka* at Cooktown; for the giant waterlily he gives *nga-wuro* for the tuber and *mumba* for the seed at Cooktown and Cape Bedford; on the Morehead River young and old plants had different names [ref:roth1901]. Palmer's Mitchell River names: *Amuma* for the blue lily, *Thoongon* for the roots, *Urgullathy* for the seed stalk and *Irrpa* for the round seed head, in a language he does not name; his Cloncurry names were *Thindah*, *Thoolambool* and *Mille* [ref:palmer1883]. Water words: **[bana](word:bana)** 'water'; **[yarru](word:yarru)** 'deep water hole'; **[dajali](word:dajali)** 'deep water'; **[mala-kural](word:mala-kural)** 'good diver' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: The lilies
sections.body:
**The blue lily**, *Nymphaea violacea*, 'is found in Australia, particularly in the Western Australian Kimberley region and in northern parts of Queensland and the Northern Territory'; 'the flowers are violet, blue or white'; 'the waterlily is a bush tucker of the Aboriginal people in northern Australia. The tuber, stem, flowers and seeds are all edible' [ref:wiki-nymphaea-violacea]. **The giant waterlily**, *N. gigantea*, is the big one of the east and north. 'The giant waterlily has a rhizomatous growth habit, that is, the main stem of the plant grows horizontally under the ground (in this case in the mud at the bottom of a lake or pond) and only the leaves and flowers are seen above the surface. The rhizome is globose, the large floating leaves are orbicular'. 'The large flowers are solitary and up to 25 cm diameter. They are held on a rigid, upright peduncle that may extend up to 50 cm above the water surface'. 'After fertilisation of the flower it is drawn underwater by the contraction of the peduncle, where the fruit ripens just below the surface. They are roughly the size of an apple and may contain up to 3,000 seeds'. 'Flowering occurs throughout the year, but is more common in warmer months. The flowers are open during the day and closed at night'. 'The habitat is permanent and semi-permanent waters of lakes, billabongs, and sluggish rivers where the bottom is deep mud and the water depth is at least 1.5 m'. 'Various parts of *Nymphaea gigantea* are edible and the plant was an important staple food for indigenous Australians across the northern parts of Australia. The golfball-sized tubers were collected from the muddy bottoms of water bodies by indigenous women and roasted before eating' [ref:wiki-nymphaea-gigantea].

**Roth's account, 1901.** '*Nymphaea caerulea*: (1.) Rhizome roasted. (2.) The seeds are baked in their pods, in "ovens" made of stones or pieces of ant-bed, covered with strips of tea-tree bark, over which ashes and sand are placed. When the pods become soft, the seeds are ready for eating (with their husks). The husks, however, may be removed by baking somewhat longer, rinsing the seeds in water (when some of the husks will float to the surface), pouring off the water, and grinding the mass between two stones. The mass is rinsed again, and ground again, and so alternately rinsed and ground, until such time as the water from the pasty mass is comparatively clear.' And of the giant lily: 'Rhizome and seed eaten: prepared like *N. caerulea*. E. Palmer says that the porous seed-stalk is peeled and eaten raw, also roasted' [ref:roth1901].

**Palmer's account, 1883, on the Mitchell.** 'The blue water-lily. Large broad leaf, floating on the surface of the water, green on the upper and blue on the under surface ... Flowers large and bluish, or blue, or white; grows in large lagoons on the Mitchell and Norman Rivers. The porous seed-stalk is peeled and eaten raw, also roasted, as well as the round seed-head, making a distinction between those containing brown or black seeds, rejecting those with light-coloured seeds. The large rough tubers growing in the mud with the floating leaves attached are roasted, being not unlike a potato, but yellow and dry when cooked' [ref:palmer1883].

**The other water plants.** The pink lotus, *Nelumbo*, whose twenty to thirty-five seeds in a flat-topped head 'are broken with a stone, and eaten raw', grew in 'large permanent lagoons, near King's Plains, Cooktown' [ref:palmer1883] [ref:roth1901]. The small fringed yellow water-snowflake (*Nymphoides*) has 'small round tubers roasted for food', and the *Aponogeton* of shallow lagoons on the Cloncurry and Mitchell has spherical bulbs an inch across 'eaten raw and roasted' [ref:palmer1883].

sections.heading: Lily, lotus, snowflake
sections.body:
- **Blue lily** (*Nymphaea*): round floating leaves with a notch, flowers blue, violet or white held above the water, the pod pulled under to ripen; tuber, stalk, flower and seed all food [ref:wiki-nymphaea-gigantea] [ref:wiki-nymphaea-violacea].
- **Pink lotus** (*Nelumbo*): leaves held up on stalks out of the water, big pink flowers, a flat-topped seed head like 'a wasp's nest'; seeds eaten raw [ref:palmer1883].
- **Water snowflake** (*Nymphoides*): small heart-shaped floating leaves and small fringed yellow flowers; small roasted tubers [ref:palmer1883].
- **Spider lily** (*jakari*): a land plant of the sand with long strap leaves and white spidery flowers; not a water lily [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Pale-seeded pods** were rejected on the Mitchell; the brown and black seeds are the ripe ones [ref:palmer1883].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **A lagoon covered in round leaves** with flowers standing above them by day and closed at night [ref:wiki-nymphaea-gigantea].
- **Flowers gone and stalks curled under**: the pods are ripening below the surface [ref:wiki-nymphaea-gigantea].
- **Jacanas walking on the pads**, the 'lilytrotter', eating seeds and insects off the floating leaves; magpie geese grazing the margins [ref:wiki-jacana] [ref:wiki-magpie-goose].
- **Dug mud and floating torn leaves** at the edge of a lagoon where tubers have been pulled [ref:wiki-nymphaea-gigantea].
- **'The shadow or long streaky film of fine bubbles'** that Roth's watchers looked for: a crocodile moving under the pads [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Where they grow
sections.body: Still, deep, muddy water: 'permanent and semi-permanent waters of lakes, billabongs, and sluggish rivers where the bottom is deep mud and the water depth is at least 1.5 m' for the giant lily; Palmer's blue lily grew 'in large lagoons on the Mitchell and Norman Rivers' [ref:wiki-nymphaea-gigantea] [ref:palmer1883]. The lotus is a coastal-lagoon plant in Palmer's record [ref:palmer1883].

sections.heading: The lily lagoon
sections.body: A lily lagoon feeds everything. The magpie goose eats 'dry grass blades, grass seeds, spike rush' and the bulbs and seeds of the wetland, and swims its goslings through the pads; the comb-crested jacana 'eats seeds and aquatic insects gleaned from floating vegetation'; the [freshwater turtles](entry:freshwater-turtle) graze the stems and open the [mussels](entry:mussels) in the mud; the [catfish](entry:catfish) and the [cherabin](entry:cherabin) work the bottom under the leaves [ref:wiki-magpie-goose] [ref:wiki-jacana] [ref:turtle-competition]. The pod sinks to ripen, so the seed is harvested from under the water, which is where the crocodile comes in: at Princess Charlotte Bay, when diving for lily seed in a suspected pool, 'there always being some friend of his or hers watching, either from the banks or an overhanging tree', who splashed the water with a stick at the first sign and 'so gives the signal to the individual below' [ref:roth1910]. The [waterhole](entry:waterhole) page sets the lagoon's year out in full.

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: 'Lilies and honey in the dry season; roots and fruits in the wet season', Roth wrote of the north generally [ref:roth1901]. The lilies flower through the year and most in the warm months, the pods follow the flowers, and the lagoons shrink through the dry until the tubers are within reach of a wading woman [ref:wiki-nymphaea-gigantea]. Palmer: the Mitchell lagoons held the blue lily, and the wild rice on the plains came with the wet [ref:palmer1883]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Tubers** roasted, 'not unlike a potato, but yellow and dry' [ref:palmer1883] [ref:roth1901].
- **Flower stalks**, porous, peeled and eaten raw or roasted [ref:palmer1883].
- **Flowers**, eaten [ref:wiki-nymphaea-violacea].
- **Seed pods** baked whole in an oven of stones or ant-bed under teatree bark [ref:roth1901].
- **Seeds**, husked by rinsing and grinding into a paste [ref:roth1901].
- **Lotus seeds** broken with a stone and eaten raw; snowflake tubers and *Aponogeton* bulbs roasted [ref:palmer1883].

sections.heading: Gathering and cooking lilies
sections.body:
From Roth and Palmer [ref:roth1901] [ref:palmer1883]:

1. **Check the lagoon** for crocodile sign before anyone goes in, and keep a watcher on the bank or in a tree while people are in the water [ref:roth1910] [ref:crocwise].
2. **Tubers**: wade or dive to the mud, follow the leaf stalks down and pull the tubers; roast them in the ashes [ref:wiki-nymphaea-gigantea] [ref:palmer1883].
3. **Stalks**: pull the flower stalks, peel them and eat raw, or roast [ref:palmer1883].
4. **Pods**: take the ripened pods from under the surface, choosing those with brown or black seeds and leaving the pale ones [ref:palmer1883] [ref:wiki-nymphaea-gigantea].
5. **Bake the pods** in an [oven](entry:earth-oven) of hot stones or ant-bed lumps, covered with strips of teatree bark, then ashes and sand, until the pods are soft; the seeds can be eaten then, husks and all [ref:roth1901].
6. **To husk**, bake longer, then rinse the seeds in water so the husks float off, pour the water away, grind the mass between two stones, rinse and grind again 'until such time as the water from the pasty mass is comparatively clear' [ref:roth1901].
7. **Lotus**: break the seeds out of the flat head with a stone and eat them raw [ref:palmer1883].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- **Crocodiles.** Every lily lagoon on a northern river is crocodile water; Roth's rule was a watcher on the bank and never a swim on the surface 'when crocodiles are about'; the Queensland rule is to be Crocwise in croc country [ref:roth1910] [ref:crocwise].
- **Pale seeds** were rejected on the Mitchell [ref:palmer1883].
- **Stagnant water**: tubers from a drying, fouled lagoon are not worth it.
- Gathering on native title country is protected by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* [ref:alrc] [ref:wyac2020].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The blue lily is a bush tucker across northern Australia wherever people still gather [ref:wiki-nymphaea-violacea]. Roth's Bloomfield name, *de-kir*, and the dictionary's *kababina* are words to check with speakers in each place [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982]; the place sections above have what is known locally.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: *[kababina](word:kababina)* 'fresh water lily'; *[jakari](word:jakari)* 'spiderlily'; *[bana](word:bana)* 'water'; *[yarru](word:yarru)* 'deep water hole'; *[dajali](word:dajali)* 'deep water'; *[mala-kural](word:mala-kural)* 'good diver'; *[bilngkumu](word:bilngkumu)* 'salt water crocodile' [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: Lilies need still water, so in the Hann country they are in the lagoons and swamps, above all in Rinyirru's wetlands, rather than in the running sandy river. The Atlas of Living Australia holds 45 water-lily records, 127 of the little water snowflakes and 10 of the pink lotus around the middle Hann [ref:ala-hann-lilies]. Roth wrote down lily names from the Morehead River and the Palmer, and today feral pigs dig the bulbs on Rinyirru [ref:roth1901] [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013].

sections.heading: Where they grow here
sections.body: The Atlas of Living Australia holds 45 *Nymphaea* records from a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru, from 1971 to 2026: *N. immutabilis* 14, *N. atrans* 13, the blue lily *N. violacea* 4, and one each of the giant waterlily *N. gigantea*, *N. carpentariae* and *N. macrosperma*, with 11 not named to species. It also holds 127 records of the water snowflakes (*Nymphoides*, 1965–2026) and 10 of the pink lotus (*Nelumbo nucifera*, 1999–2024) [ref:ala-hann-lilies]. The box takes in Rinyirru's lagoons, so read it as 'these lilies grow in this country', not as a map. Lagoons and swamps are one of the nine kinds of country the Kuku Thaypan Elders name, and in their lagoon country 'Nelumbo nucifera, water lilies Nymphaea sp., Eleocharis sp. and Oryza spp. also occur' [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: Their year here
sections.body: In the wet (December to March) the rivers flood over the plains; from about April the floodplains and wetlands dry out, and by October 'the land is brown and parched' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The lagoons shrink with them. On Rinyirru 'Feral pigs Sus scrofa occur in large numbers' and 'eat the bulbs of water lilies and turtle eggs' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013]: a rooted-up lagoon edge in the dry is pig work. See [pigs](entry:pigs).

sections.heading: How people used them here
sections.body:
**Morehead River and middle Palmer, c. 1900.** Roth's food list gives the blue lily under its local names: the Koko-rarmul of the Morehead River had two names for the rhizome, 'according as they are young or old specimens', *taro-uma* and *andu-emma*, and called the seeds *yarbadtha* and the giant waterlily *ducha-ra*; the Koko-minni of the middle Palmer called the rhizome *alkar-ma* and the seeds *acha-ra* [ref:roth1901]. He gives no separate method for these districts; his roasting and seed-baking method is in the general section above.

**Princess Charlotte Bay, c. 1900.** Lily seed was dived for in crocodile water, 'there always being some friend of his or hers watching, either from the banks or an overhanging tree' [ref:roth1910]. Both crocodiles live in the Hann country: see [crocodiles](entry:crocodiles).

**Today's evidence.** The 2023 Thaypan and Possum evidence to the Federal Court lists bush foods but does not mention lilies [ref:fca-thaypan] [ref:fca-possum]. A Koko-warra story Roth recorded at Princess Charlotte Bay has lily roots roasting in the ashes; it belongs to its custodians and is not retold here [ref:roth1903].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country, both determined in November 2023 [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]. Rinyirru is jointly managed by the Rinyirru Aboriginal Corporation and the Queensland Government, and its Traditional Owners are the Lama Lama and Kuku Thaypan peoples [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. Gathering for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal needs is part of native title [ref:nta1993].

locations.summary: At [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) the blue lily *N. violacea* is in the records, in the lagoons and backwaters off the sandy river rather than in it [ref:ala-karma-plants].

sections.heading: On the record here
sections.body: The blue lily, *Nymphaea violacea*, is the water lily recorded within 30 km of Karma Waters [ref:ala-karma-plants].

sections.heading: Where to look here
sections.body: The Mitchell at Karma Waters is mostly sand and rock pools, which is not lily ground; the blue lily record within 30 km is from the lagoons and backwaters off the river, and that is where to look [ref:ala-karma-plants] [ref:re9314].

sections.heading: Safety here
sections.body: - **Crocodiles.** At Karma Waters the resident is the [freshwater crocodile](entry:freshwater-crocodile), which is smaller and shyer but not harmless [ref:kw-about].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The blue lily is still in the lagoons of the Mitchell catchment and is a staple across the north wherever people still gather; the Bloomfield name Roth wrote down, *de-kir*, is a word to check against Western Yalanji speakers, as is *kababina* [ref:wiki-nymphaea-violacea] [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982]. Which lagoons near Karma Waters carry it, and in what months the pods are full, is for the contribution box below [ref:ala-karma-plants].
